content.text: The visible light that allows us to see the world around us is only a tiny fraction of a much broader family of waves called electromagnetic (EM) waves. From the radio waves that carry your favourite music to your car stereo, to the gamma rays emitted by radioactive nuclei, electromagnetic waves span an enormous range of wavelengths and frequencies. Despite their vast differences in energy and behaviour, all electromagnetic waves share the same fundamental nature: they are transverse waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, and they all travel at the speed of light in a vacuum.

Understanding the electromagnetic spectrum is essential for modern life. Almost every aspect of modern technology, from mobile phones and Wi-Fi to medical imaging and satellite communication, depends on our ability to generate, detect, and use different types of electromagnetic radiation. In this lesson, we will explore the full electromagnetic spectrum, learn the properties and applications of each type of radiation, and understand the dangers associated with different parts of the spectrum.

Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and perpendicular to the direction of wave travel. Unlike mechanical waves (such as sound and water waves), electromagnetic waves do not require a medium to travel through. They can propagate through a vacuum, which is how energy from the Sun reaches the Earth across 150 million kilometres of empty space.
All electromagnetic waves share these properties:
They travel at the speed of light in a vacuum:
They can travel through a vacuum (no medium required).
They can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, and polarised.
The electromagnetic spectrum is the complete range of all possible frequencies (or wavelengths) of electromagnetic radiation, arranged in order.

Properties of Each Type of Electromagnetic Radiation
Greater than about 0.1 m (from about 10 cm to many kilometres)

Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies in the EM spectrum. They can travel long distances and can diffract around obstacles such as buildings and hills. They are easily generated by oscillating electric circuits and can pass through most non-metallic materials.
Broadcasting: AM and FM radio, television signals.
Astronomy: radio telescopes detect radio waves from distant galaxies and stars.
MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging): radio waves are used in combination with strong magnetic fields to produce detailed images of the inside of the body.

Radio waves at the power levels used in broadcasting and communication are generally considered safe. Very high-power radio waves can cause heating of body tissues, but this is not a concern at normal exposure levels.
Approximately 1 mm to 0.1 m (1 mm to 10 cm)
Microwaves are short-wavelength radio waves. They can be focused into narrow beams and are absorbed by water molecules, causing heating.
Microwave ovens: microwaves at a frequency of about 2.45 GHz are absorbed by water molecules in food, causing them to vibrate and generate heat.
Satellite communication: microwaves can pass through the atmosphere and are used for transmitting signals to and from satellites.
Mobile phone networks: mobile phones communicate using microwave signals.
Radar: microwaves are used to detect the position and speed of aircraft, ships, and weather systems.
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi: these use microwave frequencies for short-range wireless communication.
Microwaves can cause internal heating of body tissues, particularly tissues with high water content. This is why microwave ovens are shielded with metal casings and mesh screens.
Microwave receivers and aerials; thermometers can detect the heating effect.
Infrared (IR) radiation is emitted by all warm objects. The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it emits. Infrared can be felt as heat when it is absorbed by the skin.
Thermal imaging cameras: detect infrared radiation to produce images showing heat patterns. Used by firefighters, the military, and in building inspections.
Remote controls: TV remote controls use infrared signals.
Heating: infrared heaters and lamps provide warmth.
Night vision: infrared cameras can "see" warm objects in the dark.
Optical fibre communication: some optical fibres use infrared signals.
Cooking: grills and toasters use infrared radiation.
Excessive exposure to infrared radiation can cause skin burns and tissue damage. Prolonged exposure can damage the eyes, particularly the cornea and lens.
Infrared sensors, thermometers, photographic film sensitive to IR, thermistors, and the skin (which feels warmth).

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum that the human eye can detect. It ranges from red (longest wavelength, lowest frequency) to violet (shortest wavelength, highest frequency). Visible light is emitted by very hot objects (such as the Sun and incandescent bulbs) and by certain electronic transitions in atoms (such as in LEDs and fluorescent lamps).
Vision: the human eye detects visible light, enabling us to see.
Very intense visible light can damage the retina of the eye. Laser light is particularly dangerous because it is highly concentrated.
The human eye, photographic film, photodiodes, CCD sensors (in cameras), and LDRs (light-dependent resistors).

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation has higher energy than visible light. It is emitted by the Sun and by special UV lamps. Many substances fluoresce (glow) when exposed to UV light, absorbing UV and re-emitting visible light.
Sterilisation: UV light kills bacteria and viruses, and is used to sterilise surgical instruments, water supplies, and food preparation surfaces.
Fluorescent lamps: UV light produced inside the tube causes the phosphor coating to fluoresce, producing visible light.
Security marking: UV-sensitive inks are used on banknotes and security documents.
Detecting forged documents: UV light can reveal hidden markings.
Sunbeds: controlled UV exposure for tanning (though this carries health risks).
Curing dental fillings and certain adhesives.

UV radiation can cause sunburn, premature skin ageing, and skin cancer with prolonged or excessive exposure. It can also damage the eyes, potentially causing cataracts. The ozone layer in Earth's atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV radiation.
UV-sensitive photographic film, fluorescent materials, photodiodes sensitive to UV.

X-rays have high energy and can penetrate soft tissues but are absorbed by dense materials such as bone and metal. They are produced when high-speed electrons are decelerated rapidly (as in an X-ray tube).
Medical imaging: X-ray photographs reveal bones and can show fractures, dental problems, and some tumours.
CT (computed tomography) scans: multiple X-ray images taken from different angles are combined by a computer to create detailed cross-sectional images.
Airport security: X-ray scanners examine luggage for prohibited items.
Industrial inspection: X-rays are used to check welds, castings, and other structures for internal defects.
Crystallography: X-ray diffraction is used to determine the atomic structure of crystals and molecules.

X-rays are ionising radiation, meaning they carry enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and damage living cells. Excessive exposure can cause cell damage, mutations, and cancer. Medical X-ray exposure is kept as low as reasonably achievable (the ALARA principle), and radiographers use lead shielding and stand behind protective barriers.
Photographic film (X-rays darken the film), fluorescent screens, electronic detectors (CCD sensors).

Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, highest frequencies, and highest energies in the EM spectrum. They are emitted by radioactive nuclei during nuclear decay processes. Gamma rays are highly penetrating and can pass through most materials, although they are attenuated by thick lead or concrete.
Cancer treatment (radiotherapy): targeted beams of gamma rays are used to destroy cancer cells.
Sterilisation: gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and food products.
Medical imaging: gamma cameras detect gamma rays emitted by radioactive tracers injected into the body (nuclear medicine).
Astronomy: gamma-ray telescopes detect gamma rays from extreme cosmic events such as supernovae and black holes.
Industrial gauging: gamma rays are used to measure the thickness of materials.

Gamma rays are the most dangerous form of EM radiation because of their very high energy and penetrating ability. They can cause severe cell damage, radiation sickness, genetic mutations, and cancer. Strict safety measures, including thick lead shielding and minimised exposure times, are essential when working with gamma ray sources.
Geiger-Muller tubes, photographic film, scintillation detectors, semiconductor detectors.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum:

This is one of the fundamental constants of physics. In other media (such as glass, water, or air), EM waves travel slightly slower, and different frequencies may travel at slightly different speeds (which is what causes dispersion, as studied in the previous lesson).
Electromagnetic radiation can be broadly divided into two categories based on its energy:
(radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light) does not carry enough energy per photon to remove electrons from atoms. Its main effect on matter is heating.

(ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays) carries enough energy per photon to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions. This can break chemical bonds in molecules, including DNA, leading to cell damage, mutations, and cancer. This is why these types of radiation require careful handling and shielding.
The boundary between ionising and non-ionising radiation falls approximately at the ultraviolet region of the spectrum.

Misconception 1: Different EM waves travel at different speeds
In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at exactly the same speed:

m/s. Radio waves, light, X-rays, and gamma rays all travel at the speed of light. The differences between them are in their wavelength and frequency, not their speed. In a medium like glass, different frequencies may travel at slightly different speeds, but in a vacuum, the speed is universal.

Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, not sound waves. They travel at the speed of light, not the speed of sound, and they can travel through a vacuum. A radio receiver converts radio wave signals into sound waves that we can hear, but the waves travelling through the air from the broadcasting tower to your radio are electromagnetic, not acoustic.
Misconception 3: Microwaves are only used in microwave ovens

While microwave ovens are perhaps the most well-known application, microwaves are used extensively in telecommunications (mobile phones, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, satellite links) and in radar systems. The microwave region of the spectrum is one of the most heavily utilised in modern technology.
Misconception 4: All electromagnetic radiation is dangerous

The danger of electromagnetic radiation depends on its frequency (energy per photon) and the intensity of exposure. Low-frequency, non-ionising radiation (radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light) is generally safe at normal exposure levels. The primary danger is from ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays), which can damage DNA and cause cancer. Even with ionising radiation, the risk depends on the dose and duration of exposure.
Misconception 5: Gamma rays and X-rays are completely different

Gamma rays and X-rays overlap in wavelength and frequency. The distinction between them is based on their origin, not their properties. X-rays are typically produced by electron transitions and deceleration, while gamma rays are emitted by atomic nuclei. A gamma ray and an X-ray of the same wavelength are physically identical.

The EM spectrum, in order of decreasing wavelength, is: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
Each type of EM radiation has characteristic properties, uses, and associated dangers.
Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and are used for broadcasting and communication.
Microwaves are used in cooking, mobile phones, Wi-Fi, and satellite communication.
Infrared is associated with heat and is used in thermal imaging and remote controls.
Visible light is the only EM radiation detectable by the human eye.
Ultraviolet causes sunburn and is used for sterilisation and fluorescence.
X-rays penetrate soft tissue and are used in medical imaging.
Gamma rays are the most energetic and penetrating; they are used in cancer treatment and sterilisation.
Non-ionising radiation (radio to visible) mainly causes heating. Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) can damage DNA and cause cancer.

(a) X-rays are used to detect broken bones because they can penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone. This produces a shadow image on a detector, showing the bone structure and any fractures.
(b) Microwaves are used for cooking because they are absorbed by water molecules in food, causing the molecules to vibrate faster and generate heat, cooking the food from within.
(c) Microwaves are used for satellite communication because they can pass through the Earth's atmosphere with minimal absorption and can be focused into narrow beams aimed at the satellite.

(d) Gamma rays are used for sterilising surgical equipment because their very high energy can kill bacteria and other microorganisms. They are highly penetrating, so they can sterilise equipment sealed in packaging.

(e) Visible light allows you to see this page. Light from a source reflects off the page (diffuse reflection). The reflected light enters your eye, where it is focused onto the retina, producing an image.
Gamma rays have much higher frequencies than radio waves. Although both travel at the same speed (

m/s), higher-frequency electromagnetic radiation is ionising, meaning it carries enough energy to remove electrons from atoms in living tissue. This ionisation can break chemical bonds in DNA molecules, causing cell damage, mutations, and potentially cancer. Radio waves have very low frequencies and are non-ionising; their main effect is slight heating, which is negligible at normal exposure levels and does not damage cells or DNA.
